articles.title: Giannis Leads Heat Past Rockets Amid Bam Injury, Box Score Stats, Highlights for Durant, Top Players
articles.summary: There was good news and there was bad news for the Miami Heat on Monday night.
articles.body:
There was good news and there was bad news for the Miami Heat on Monday night.

The good news was that the team cruised to a 128-110 victory over the Houston Rockets. The bad news was that star center Bam Adebayo didn't play in the second half due to hip tightness.

The hope, obviously, is that the injury is a minor one and his second-half absence was precautionary. In either event, the Heat pulled off the win against a tough Houston team. Here's a look at the game's key performers

Giannis Antetokounmpo helped pick up the slack in the second half after he got off to a slow offensive start in the first two quarters.

It helped that Klay Thompson was on fire from three (5-of-8). And the Heat's backups were superb, outscoring Houston's second unit by a 57-38 margin.

Any team is tough to beat if they hit 18 threes or dish out 29 assists like Miami did on Monday night.

The Heat, if you'll excuse the pun, are red hot at the moment. The win over the Rockets made it five straight victories for Miami (8-6) after a 3-6 start to the season. The Giannis Era may have gotten off to a rocky start, but the Heat appear to have turned a corner, and just in time for Wednesday's matchup against Antetokounmpo's former team, the Milwaukee Bucks.

The Rockets (11-4), meanwhile, have been far better this year than they looked on Monday night. They'll look to rebound on Wednesday against the Indiana Pacers.

articles.title: Bam Adebayo leaves win over Rockets early with hip injury, Heat don't expect long-term issue
articles.summary: Despite losing Bam Adebayo in the second half, the Heat still rolled to a 128-110 win over the Rockets on Monday night.
articles.body:
Bam Adebayo left Monday night's game against the Houston Rockets early with an apparent hip injury.

The Miami Heat star did not take the court to start the second half of their 128-110 victory over the Rockets at the Kaseya Center on Monday, and was instead replaced by Andrew Wiggins to open the third quarter. It didn't appear as if anything happened to Adebayo in the first half, but he was not spotted on the bench as play resumed.

Eventually, the Heat said he was questionable to return with right hip tightness. They then ruled him out for good in the fourth quarter. Further specifics of the injury are not yet known.

Adebayo finished the night with just four points and two assists while shooting 1 of 3 from the field. He entered the night averaging 19.5 points and 8.5 rebounds per contest this season.

Heat coach Erik Spoelstra said after the game that the team was being "proactive" in holding Adebayo out, and that he didn't expect it to be a long-term issue, according to the Miami Herald's Anthony Chiang .

"I saw how he was grinding through it in the second quarter," Spoelstra said, via ESPN . "No matter what he says and no matter what anybody says, let's sit him down and evaluate him tomorrow."

While they don't have specifics yet, losing Adebayo for an extended amount of time would undoubtedly make a major impact on the Heat. Despite losing him, the Heat still managed to roll to a convincing win over the Rockets.

Miami led nearly the entire way on Monday night. The Heat carried a 16-point lead into the locker room at halftime and just cruised the rest of the way to secure the 18-point victory. Giannis Antetokounmpo led the way with 20 points, 16 rebounds and 6 assists. Klay Thompson added 17 points after going 5 of 10 from the 3-point line, and Wiggins had 17 points and five rebounds after stepping in for Adebayo in the second half. The Heat have now won five straight, and sit at 8-6 on the season.

Alperen Sengun led the Rockets with 23 points and seven rebounds. Kevin Durant finished with 22 points, and Jabari Smith Jr. had 12 points and 10 rebounds. The loss dropped them to 11-4 on the year.

articles.title: Bill Fennelly: Iowa State head coach suspended for one game for pushing Sienna Harvey on head
articles.summary: University basketball coach Bill Fennelly is given a one-game suspension for pushing a female player on the head during a timeout.
articles.body:
A university basketball coach in the United States has been given a one-game suspension for pushing a female player on the head during a timeout.

Players were huddled around Iowa State women's coach Bill Fennelly during a fourth-quarter timeout on Sunday when the 69-year-old spoke to guard Sienna Harvey and pushed her on the forehead.

Australian Harvey did not react to the incident, and the Iowa State Cyclones won 69-64 against the University of Illinois-Chicago Flames.

Following the game, Iowa State athletics took disciplinary action against Fennelly, who is now suspended for the Cyclones' next fixture against Northern Iowa on Wednesday.

Fennelly apologised to Harvey, her family and team-mates and said he had allowed his emotions to get the better of him.

"I fully recognise that there are no situations where it is appropriate to make contact with a student-athlete in that way," he said in a statement.

"I accept responsibility and will serve the suspension and I will do better moving forward."

Iowa State athletic director Jared Benko said: "We cannot tolerate inappropriate contact between a coach or staff member and a student-athlete in practice or in competition, whether intentional or not."

Fennelly, who joined Iowa State as women's head coach in 1995, announced in October he plans to retire at the end of the season - his 32nd with the Cyclones.

articles.title: Is Luka Doncic already matching prime LeBron James? Former Cavaliers teammate offers his definitive take
articles.summary: Luka Doncic is averaging 39.0 points per game, and DeMarcus Cousins believes the Los Angeles Lakers superstar has not hit his ceiling.
articles.body: Luka Doncic is averaging 39.0 points per game, and DeMarcus Cousins believes the Los Angeles Lakers superstar has not hit his ceiling. The former All-Star made the case on Gil’s Arena, where he argued with Gilbert Arenas over a hypothetical: Doncic’s Lakers against LeBron James and the 2007 Cleveland Cavaliers. Arenas took James, whom he faced in the playoffs. Cousins took Doncic, and he expects bigger scoring nights once the Lakers star reaches midseason form. The Lakers are 12-2 after eight straight wins, with Doncic putting up 43 against the Phoenix Suns last Sunday.Is Luka Doncic already on prime LeBron James’ level?Nobody in the debate claimed Luka Doncic has passed LeBron James. DeMarcus Cousins and Arenas were arguing over how a team built around each star would fare. James carried a thin Cleveland roster to the 2007 NBA Finals in his fourth season, and Arenas wanted that version respected.His point was simple. Most people picture a 30-year-old or 40-year-old James, not the 21- or 22-year-old he played against. “Who the f*** is stopping LeBron James?” Arenas asked.Cousins first asked whether the point was stopping James or containing him. He agreed James is incredible. Still, Cousins sees “nothing that can stop Luka” out there.Both teams leaned hard on one star, so the matchup is tough to settle on paper. Cleveland does not reach the Finals without James.The gap between the two cases is clear. James has a Finals trip from 2007. Doncic has a 12-2 start and the best 12-game scoring total in 50 years, but the season is only 14 games old.Doncic’s numbers back up Cousins’ 100-point talkCousins also believes Doncic is only warming up. He would not be shocked by a 100-point game from Doncic soon, and he named Wilt Chamberlain’s record as the mark in play.The numbers make the talk reasonable. Doncic has 468 points through 12 games, the most for any player over that span in 50 years. Seven of those games went for 40 or more, which is 25 percent of all 40-point games league-wide this season. He has two 50-point nights, and his lowest total is 23.Doncic averaged 36.2 points in October and has pushed that to 41.0 in November, shooting 49.4 percent from the field, 41.8 percent from three and 85.9 percent at the line. If the 39.0 average holds, he joins Michael Jordan, Kobe Bryant and James Harden as the only players to average 35 or more in a season since 1980.Tim Hardaway sees it the same way, with a condition. He said if anyone can get there, it is Doncic, but health decides it. Doncic played only 50 and 64 games in the last two seasons.Doncic was not sold when Cousins asked him about 100 at the 2026 All-Star weekend. “I scored 73, and it was a lot,” he said. Nine months on, he is hotter, and the Lakers roster around him fits his scoring better.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: New NBA Trade Rumors on Thunder's Plans After Chet Holmgren, Jalen Williams Injuries
articles.summary: Despite an up and down start to the season amid significant injuries to key players, the Oklahoma City Thunder aren't in a rush to add frontcourt help with Chet Holmgren expected to miss at least another month.
articles.body:
Despite an up and down start to the season amid significant injuries to key players, the Oklahoma City Thunder aren't in a rush to add frontcourt help with Chet Holmgren expected to miss at least another month.

Per NBA insider Marc Stein , the Thunder are "bullish on the idea" that Isaiah Hartenstein, Jaylin Williams and Aday Mara can hold things down until Holmgren is able to return.

This comes after Oklahoma City general manager Sam Presti traded two second-round picks to the Sacramento Kings for Nique Clifford to add wing depth with Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace out indefinitely due to injuries.

Biggest NBA Surprises and Disappointments 🏀

"The early word is that Oklahoma City doesn't feel the same imminent pressure to fortify its frontcourt after Chet Holmgren also went down," Stein wrote. "The Thunder are said to be bullish on the idea that Isaiah Hartenstein, Jaylin Williams and rookie big man Aday Mara can meet the team's frontcourt needs until Holmgren's return."

One key difference between Holmgren's situation and the Williams-Wallace injuries is the former has a projected return timeline.

The Thunder announced on Oct. 30 that Holmgren was starting a treatment plan for a small patellar tendon tear and he would be re-evaluated in eight to 10 weeks.

Williams had surgery to repair a fractured fibula and dislocated left ankle suffered on Oct. 25. Wallace had surgery for a torn labrum on Oct. 30. Neither player has been officially ruled out for the season at this point, but they are expected to require lengthy rehabs.

There are also potential financial reasons for the Thunder to be patient since it's still early in the season. They are only $3.5 million under the second apron, so they don't have a lot of wiggle room to make additions that might add salary to their payroll without hitting that threshold.

It also helps that the players covering Holmgren's minutes have done well so far this season. Mara, the No. 12 pick in the 2026 NBA draft, has looked good out of the gate with 9.1 points, 6.5 rebounds and 1.7 blocks per game in 21.6 minutes per game in 14 appearances.

Thunder head coach Mark Daigneault has started Mara in four of the last seven games. Hartenstein remains solid in his role as a rim protector, averaging 8.6 points and 10.6 rebounds per game in 14 starts.

Williams hasn't played since Nov. 2 due to a lower-back injury, but he has been an effective bench contributor for the Thunder throughout his career.

The eight-to-10-week timeline for Holmgren means the earliest he could be back is around Christmas.

As long as the Thunder can continue to tread water waiting for Holmgren to return, they can afford to be patient. Their record sits at 9-5 going into Wednesday's game against the Atlanta Hawks.

articles.title: Steph Curry Opens Up on 'Basketball Mortality' and Warriors Being 'Any Semblance of a Threat'
articles.summary: As the Golden State Warriors try to hold their head above water with Stephen Curry out for the time being due to an oblique abdominal tear, the two-time NBA MVP has let his thoughts occasionally drift toward the end of his career.
articles.body:
As the Golden State Warriors try to hold their head above water with Stephen Curry out for the time being due to an oblique abdominal tear, the two-time NBA MVP has let his thoughts occasionally drift toward the end of his career.

Speaking to ESPN's Anthony Slater , Curry acknowledged his latest injury is another reminder of his "basketball mortality" because the end of the road is getting closer even though he was playing at a high level prior to the getting hurt.

"It sucks because it's a part of your mortality," Curry said. "Basketball mortality."

Biggest NBA Surprises and Disappointments 🏀

One thing that Curry is well aware of is the Warriors needing him to be available if they are going to be "any semblance of a threat" to win a championship this season.

"If we want to be any semblance of a threat come the end of the year, I need to be available," Curry told Slater.

Curry injured his oblique in the first quarter of Golden State's 115-108 loss to the Houston Rockets on Nov. 11. The Warriors announced he would be re-evaluated in two weeks, with ESPN's Shams Charania reporting the expectation is he will miss close to a month.

In their two games without Curry so far, the Warriors are 0-2 and have been outscored by a combined 57 points. They were held under 100 points in both games, including 94 against a New Orleans Pelicans team that had given up at least 113 points in their previous eight games.

Curry admitted to Slater watching Jimmy Butler originally tear his ACL during a game in January last season left him thinking about the future and what it might look like.

"I saw him go down, Jimmy [Butler] go down [in January]. You look at the calendar," Curry said. "Then, you start thinking about more of the existential part of it. Will I have to deal with this the rest of my career? Is it something that will ... what's the word ... will it diminish what I'm able to do on the court?"

There has been hope to start this season thanks in large part to the immediate impact of Yaxel Lendeborg, the No. 11 pick in the 2026 NBA draft, and what he added on both ends of the court.

Adding to the frustration of Curry's latest injury is he looked like a potential MVP candidate prior to it. He was averaging 34.0 points on 47.2 percent three-point shooting, 5.2 assists and 5.0 rebounds in six games before the Houston matchup.

"I know how blessed I am to even still have the ability to convince myself that I could be the best player on a championship-contending team," Curry said of his early-season play.

The combination of Curry playing at that level and Lendeborg had the Warriors sitting at 8-3 after 11 games and giving them some runway to imagine what things might look like when Butler returns. The Warriors have lost three of four games without Curry in 2026-27.

This season is far from over and there will be plenty of time remaining when Curry returns, assuming he is back within a month, but his injury is a reminder of how fragile things are for the Warriors because he has missed a lot of time since the start of the 2025-26 season.

articles.title: Steph Curry Addresses NBA Retirement and Explains Pay Cut on New Warriors Contract
articles.summary: Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry knows the end of his legendary career is drawing closer.
articles.body:
Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry knows the end of his legendary career is drawing closer.

So when the four-time NBA champion faced a contract decision over the offseason, he didn't hesitate to take a slight pay cut, telling ESPN's Anthony Slater that he wanted to eliminate distractions and give the Warriors some flexibility for what could be his final two years in the league.

"All of it," Curry said. "I assumed that it would probably be one of, if not the last, contract I signed. I'm not afraid to say it. But maybe I'll surprise myself and want to keep going."

Curry agreed to a two-year, $116 million extension that gave $10 million in cap space back to the Warriors next summer and included a player option in the final year, potentially keeping him in Golden State for 20 straight seasons. While he would've been eligible for a max contract extension, the 38-year-old isn't focused on the finances at this stage in his career.

The two-time NBA MVP remains one of the best scorers in the game, but he told Slater that he would've been willing to accept a complementary role if his skills started to fade with his age. He still remains open to that possibility.

"It would not kill my ego," Curry said. "I want to win. Whatever that means, you make decisions based on what's in front of you."

Slater noted that Curry "made clear that there hasn't and won't be a retirement decision soon." However, he acknowledged that the end is coming, and he wants to enjoy it while it lasts.

"I want to appreciate what's happening right now because I don't want to just go through the motions," Curry said. "Then, it passes you by."

articles.title: Michael Jordan's Air Jordan 1 Collection and 'Last Dance' Jersey for Sale at Auction
articles.summary: Some of Michael Jordan's most iconic collectibles are up for grabs in an auction that launched on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Some of Michael Jordan's most iconic collectibles are up for grabs in an auction that launched on Tuesday.

The Realest announced a landmark auction that features a game-worn Chicago Bulls jersey from Jordan's legendary 1997-1998 "Last Dance" championship season and six pairs of Air Jordan 1 sneakers. Bidding for the items will close on Dec. 12.

All six pairs of Air Jordan 1s feature the white, black and red Chicago colorway. According to a release, the pairs include:

Jordan's game-worn and signed 1985 Air Jordan 1 Player Exclusives, which previously set a Guinness World Record for the most expensive sneakers ever sold at auction

Rare game-worn, dual-signed Air Jordan 1 Strap Player Exclusives, worn during Jordan's return from a broken foot in 1986

Unworn, deadstock 1985 Air Jordan 1 Player Exclusives made specifically for Jordan

An original deadstock 1985 Air Jordan 1 Chicago retail pair

An Italian-made Air Jordan 1.5 prototype

A 2017 Off-White Air Jordan 1 Chicago pair signed and inscribed by the late Virgil Abloh

Jordan's collectibles are some of the most popular in the sports collectibles space. It was just last month that a game-worn, autographed Jordan road jersey from the 1998 NBA Finals was privately sold for $14 million, setting a new record for the highest price ever paid for a piece of basketball memorabilia.

It's safe to expect that this latest auction will fetch some eye-popping prices for Jordan's rare pieces.

articles.title: Spurs' 12-game winning streak: What to know about Victor Wembanyama and the NBA's hottest team
articles.summary: Let's highlight what's worth knowing about the Spurs' stampede to the top of the Western Conference.
articles.body:
The NBA's hottest team resides in South Texas. After knocking off the Utah Jazz in Salt Lake City on Sunday night, the San Antonio Spurs enter a new week riding a 12-game winning streak — the franchise's longest in more than a decade . Last season featured only two streaks longer than the Spurs' dominant dozen: a 16-game early-season jaunt by the Oklahoma City Thunder (which, as you might remember, these Spurs snapped in the NBA Cup semifinals ) and a 13-game run by the Detroit Pistons … who, as luck would have it, will visit the Spurs in San Antonio on Tuesday night.

When a team goes on a winning streak this long, there's plenty of credit to go around. Let's highlight 12 things worth knowing about the Spurs' stampede to the top of the Western Conference — one for each win in the streak! — starting with … I mean, come on, where else can you start?

1. Victor Wembanyama is back with a vengeance.

After the New York Knicks ended his phenomenal third season just short of a championship, Wembanyama entered the summer with a bitter taste in his mouth … and he seems to have entered the new campaign intent on washing it out by devouring everything in his path.

Wembanyama enters Tuesday's action third in the NBA in scoring (a career-high 28.6 points per game) and fifth in rebounding (11.6 caroms a night) while, for the fourth straight season, leading the league in blocked shots (4.3 swats per contest). He hasn't forsaken the 3-point arc, but he's taking a higher share of his shots than ever directly at the rim , and he's converting them at a predictably elite rate, shooting 79.5% in the restricted area — tops among players to take at least 50 point-blank shots .

(Third on that list, by the way? Friggin' Dylan Harper. Don't worry: We'll get back to him.)

Big Vic is averaging — averaging! — 4.64 dunks per game. That's nearly two more flushes per game than last season (2.78), which was already a career high. As tactics go, "Let's get the biggest guy as close to the basket as possible and let him just put the ball into it" seems like a pretty smart strategy, and the Spurs have been reaping the benefits of it, scoring a scorching 126.6 points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions in Wemby's minutes, according to Cleaning the Glass — a mark that would rank head-and-shoulders above the Los Angeles Lakers' league-leading rate of offensive efficiency thus far.

When it comes to "season-opening heaters," most of the attention has gone to the man most responsible for that No. 1-ranked Lakers offense, Luka Dončić — and understandably so . It's worth noting, though, that the big fella is currently on pace to shatter the all-time record for player efficiency rating while leading the NBA in win shares , value over replacement player and total plus-minus ; the Spurs have outscored opponents by 257 points in Wemby's 417 minutes, equivalent to a staggering 29.5 points-per-100 .

Watch Wembanyama on a nightly basis — not just the "did he just finger-roll from past the free-throw line ?!?" highlights, but the possession after possession where he completely warps the opposition's defense and defangs its offense just by standing there — and you come away feeling like the 22-year-old's control of the game is, or at least can be , total.

"Opponents can't really put me in a situation where I can't answer," Wembanyama recently told reporters . "So now all I have to do is not beat myself."

For more than three weeks, he hasn't — and, in a related story, nobody's beaten the Spurs, either.

2. Perfectly balanced , as all things should be.

All right, take it easy there, Thanos. (Not sure if you've heard, but it's all about Dr. Doom right now.)

Generally speaking, if you're in the top 10 on both ends of the floor, you can consider yourself a contender; if you're in the top five on both ends, you're in the inner circle. San Antonio enters Tuesday's action ranked second in the NBA in points scored and allowed per possession, according to Cleaning the Glass .

Where'd the Spurs finish last year, you might ask? Oh, I'm so glad you did. They were … third in points scored per possession, and third in points allowed per possession. If that was good enough to get them to the Finals, maybe bumping up to second both ways will be enough to get them to the top of the mountain this time?

3. The Spurs' start has them in some really rarefied air.

San Antonio has a point differential of +180 for the season — the 21st-highest total ever through the first 14 games of a campaign, according to Stathead . Of the 20 teams above these Spurs, 17 made at least the conference finals; eight of them won it all.

Here's another: The Spurs are blitzing their opponents by 15.2 points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions thus far — the best net rating in the sport . Since the 2003-04 season, only four teams have finished a season outscoring the opposition by more than 12 points-per-100. All four of them — the 2007-08 Boston Celtics, 2014-15 and 2016-17 Golden State Warriors, and the 2024-25 Thunder — went on to win the NBA championship.

According to Jared Dubin's adjusted efficiency metrics at Last Night in Basketball , which measure how much better or worse a team's offense and defense were than the league's average unit in that season, the 2026-27 Spurs currently have a net rating 11.4 points-per-100 better than league average. That ranks third in Dubin's database, which goes all the way back to the ABA-NBA merger in 1976 — behind only Michael Jordan's 1995-96 Chicago Bulls (who won the title) … and this year's Boston Celtics, who (Monday's loss to the Orlando Magic notwithstanding) have been pretty awesome this year.

San Antonio's average margin of victory thus far is 12.86 points per game . Only one team has ever finished a full season higher: the '24-25 Thunder ( +12.87 ) … who, again, won the title.

According to Basketball-Reference's Simple Rating System — a metric "that takes into account average point differential and strength of schedule" — this year's Spurs are 12.75 points better than league average . That's on pace to be the highest SRS rating in Basketball-Reference's database , ahead of teams like the '24-25 Thunder, 1970-71 Milwaukee Bucks, '95-96 Bulls and 1971-72 Los Angeles Lakers — all of whom (say it with me) won the title.

It's early, obviously, and 14 games is too small a sample to draw any definitive conclusions. This much, though, seems clear. If folks start digging into the historical record in search of points of comparison to what you're doing, and they keep coming up with teams that won the NBA championship? You're probably doing something right.

5. That whole three-guard lineup thing? Seems to be working OK!

The backcourt logjam that some pundits anticipated last season never really materialized in San Antonio. De'Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle started; rookie Harper mostly came off the bench; the trio shared the floor for just 25 minutes during the regular season and 44 minutes in the playoffs , and the Spurs made it all the way to the NBA Finals. Not actually a problem, right?

Well, that seemed less likely to be the case this season, after Harper authored a breakout performance in his first postseason — and followed it up by making it pretty clear that he wasn't particularly interested in continuing to come off the bench . That led Spurs head coach Mitch Johnson to decide to open this season with all three of his high-octane guards in the starting five , backstopped by Wembanyama with Devin Vassell operating as an ostensible small-ball power forward. The early returns have been explosive:

The Spurs have hammered opponents by 110 points in 141 minutes with Fox, Castle and Harper sharing the floor this season, according to PBP Stats . They're scoring and defending at league-best rates in those minutes … and yes, a lot of that stems from the fact that Wembanyama has been out there for every single one of them. It's also working, though, because the guards are each finding ways to get in where they fit in.

They're flying up the court, with more than 23% of San Antonio's offensive possessions coming in transition in the three-guard lineup, and those units scoring at near-league-best levels on the break . Castle and Harper are almost exclusively taking shots at the rim or from beyond the arc in those minutes , getting to either catch-and-shoot or attack downhill after an initial action bends the defense.

Fox and Castle, both questionable 3-point shooters, have both been knocking down well over 40% of their triples in these alignments . When the pick-your-poison wheel spins to a center guarding Castle, the Spurs have shown their work in developing counters to that scheme.

And while conventional wisdom would warn you against the defensive drawbacks of playing small, with no player listed taller than 6-foot-6 at the 1 through 4 spots, those lineups have rebounded fine, haven't given up a ton of opportunities at the rim, and have yet to be significantly exploited for their lack of size on the perimeter. (It seems that having that French dude back there goes a long way toward bucking conventional wisdom.)

"I understand the narrative around it. I always land on the same reasoning at the very end of it," Johnson told reporters about starting the three guards during the preseason. "They're three of our better players. [...] I think they can dribble, pass, shoot, defend, make winning plays."

Whether they'll continue to do so in this alignment remains to be seen; when offseason signing/veteran power forward Tobias Harris heals up from the calf injury that has cost him the opening month of the season, Johnson will likely have a difficult decision to make. Then again, if the not-so-small-ball Spurs keep blowing everybody's doors off in this look … maybe he won't.

"The biggest thing is, I've got handlers all around me — guys that we want to put the ball in their hands and pick-and-roll around me," Wembanyama said . "That makes things easier."

Since opening the season with losses to the Thunder and Rockets , the Spurs have gotten the opportunity to get right with a pretty friendly stretch of road.

They've had three games against the Jazz, two games against the Kings, and matchups with the Suns and Bulls. They've also caught the Timberwolves without Anthony Edwards or Rudy Gobert, the Mavericks without Cooper Flagg or Kyrie Irving, the Trail Blazers without Ja Morant , and the Warriors right after Stephen Curry went down .

Add it all up, and the Spurs' season-opening slate ranks among the softest in the NBA, according to multiple strength -of- schedule metrics . San Antonio doesn't have to apologize for that, of course. You play the teams that are in front of you, with whoever's in uniform for them when you show up. We've seen plenty of teams fail to capitalize on the opportunity to take down a team at less than full strength. (Looking at you, Mavs .)

Besides, when presented with matchups against shorthanded or sorry opposition, the Spurs have done what good teams are supposed to do: namely, win all of those games, with most of those victories coming by double digits. It's just something to keep an eye on, particularly with a tough opponent like Detroit up next … before three more against the Clippers, Pelicans and Kings. (The games to really keep an eye on? Nov. 27 against Luka and the Lakers, and Nov. 29 against that damn good Celtics team.)

Fox got raked over the coals this summer for his underperformance in the NBA Finals. (Which, it's worth remembering, came with him nursing a high ankle sprain that likely would've sidelined him for weeks had it been the regular season.) His struggles under the brightest lights, combined with Harper's stellar showing in his maiden postseason voyage, primed the pump for the shift to the three-guard lineup, and led to no shortage of calls for the veteran triggerman to cede the stage — and his spot in the Spurs' pecking order — to the rising sophomore.

Well, Fox is still here … and he's kind of threading the needle.

Fox has taken a clear step back in the Spurs' offensive hierarchy, averaging fewer minutes and points per game than he has since his rookie season, and posting far and away the lowest usage rate, time of possession and average number of touches of his 10-year career. He's taking seven fewer field goal attempts per 100 possessions than he did last year.

When Fox shares the floor with Harper and Castle, he's finishing just 15.7% of San Antonio's offensive possessions with a shot attempt, foul drawn or turnover — the kind of usage rate more commonly associated with a complementary player like Isaiah Hartenstein, Toumani Camara or Christian Braun than with a two-time All-Star who has averaged 21 points per game in his career. He's performing well in that reduced role, though.

Fox more frequently takes high-percentage shots — 32% of his attempts are coming at the rim, his highest rate in six years , while corner 3s account for 12% of his shots, a career high — and has almost totally excised long 2-pointers from his repertoire. That, in turn, has led to more efficient scoring. He enters Tuesday's action toting a .551 effective field goal percentage (which accounts for 3-pointers being worth more than 2-pointers) and a .621 true shooting percentage (which factors in 2-point, 3-point and free-throw accuracy) — both of which are by far the highest marks of his career.

He has paired that leaner shot diet with a voracious appetite for freebies, too, drawing shooting fouls on more than 19% of his field-goal attempts — again, a career high. In fact, among 153 players who have logged at least 300 minutes this season, Fox's .496 free-throw attempt rate is the 11th-highest in the NBA , just ahead of free-throw-magnet big men Joel Embiid and Giannis Antetokounmpo.

Pair that just-the-facts-ma'am scoring game with his ongoing facilitation — a team-high 5.8 assists per game, including 33 to Wemby, making them the third-most-frequent assist combo in the NBA thus far — and Fox has managed to continue providing value while still making room for the evolution of the young talent around him. Not bad.

8. San Antonio's dominating the transition game …

For fans of a certain age, thinking of the Spurs might evoke images of patient, methodical offensive possessions — all entry passes to Tim Duncan on the low block or swing-swing symphonies of "good-to-great" ball movement, where the pace of their play is secondary to the precision of their movements. These aren't your daddy's Spurs, though; these dudes have a predilection toward moving fast and breaking things. Like, for example, you.

In terms of overall pace of play, the Spurs rank just 24th in the NBA, with their average game featuring about 98.8 possessions, according to NBA Advanced Stats . That's due in large part to their defense, though; San Antonio has the longest average defensive possession in the NBA this season, according to PBP Stats . That stands to reason: When you've got to try to figure out how to crowbar open a crevice to attack with Wembanyama menacing along the back line while the likes of Castle and Harper pressure the ball up top, it might take you a little while.

Once the Spurs get the ball, though, they hit the gas. San Antonio has the fifth-fastest average offensive possession this season, and is tied for the fifth-quickest average time to shot, according to Inpredictable .

As noted by the great John Schuhmann , the Spurs lead the NBA in both transition points scored and allowed per game, outscoring opponents by 13 points a night on the break — a massive gap. With their ability to force turnovers, finish possessions with rebounds and advance the ball to all those jet-fueled guards, more than 19% of their offensive possessions come in transition, according to Cleaning the Glass ; that's the most in the league. But thanks to their ability to protect the defensive glass, take care of the ball and sprint back, fewer than 12% of their defensive possessions come in transition … which is also No. 1 in the league .

Since at least the start of the 2003-04 season, no team has ever finished the year No. 1 in the league at both generating and preventing transition opportunities. Just another way these Spurs are on pace (ha!) to dispense with conventional wisdom.

Winning the possession battle isn't exactly a revolutionary concept; coaches have been preaching since time immemorial the importance of taking care of the ball on offense and finishing possessions on defense. It's become an increasingly large point of emphasis in recent years, though, as front offices and coaching staffs engaged in the perpetual pursuit of optimization, hunting for every advantage on both ends of the floor. As it turns out, "making sure we get more chances to shoot and score than the other guys" is a pretty solid way to approach things!

The Spurs were pretty good at that last season. When you factor in how many offensive rebounds they pulled in against how many they gave up, how many free-throw attempts they racked up versus how many they conceded, and how many times they turned the ball over compared with how many times they forced opponents to cough it up, San Antonio generated 2.2 more offensive possessions than its opponents per game during the regular season — a good number, but not quite in the upper echelons of the league, like the team that knocked them off in the Finals.

This season, though, the Spurs have tightened the screws virtually across the board. They're grabbing an even higher share of their own missed shots, turning the ball over at the NBA's lowest rate and getting to the free-throw line more frequently, while also forcing more turnovers and curbing their foul rate. Add it up, and through 14 games, San Antonio is generating 7.2 more possessions per game than its opponents — a massive leap over last season, and the No. 1 mark in the league thus far .

Make sure you take more shots on goal than the other guys and you've got a great shot at winning a lot more often than you lose — especially when you put the ball in the hands of dudes who can make those shots. Dudes like …

… the 20-year-old sophomore, whose combination of throwback cool and downhill explosiveness just keeps leaping off the screen pretty much every time you see him.

Harper has responded to his elevation into the starting lineup by continuing to ball out. His usage, free-throw attempt rate and scoring efficiency are all up; his turnover rate is down. Some of that, obviously, comes from more frequently sharing the floor with multiple other high-level ball-handlers, but still: pretty nice to have the guy who's second on your team in touches only coughing it up 8% of the time, one of the lowest rates of any guard in the league .

Coming off that sensational rookie season, Harper is pretty firmly establishing himself as one of the best players in the league when it comes to getting into the paint and finishing on the interior, shooting a frankly bananas 78.6% in the restricted area — better than high-efficiency bigs like Domantas Sabonis, Jarrett Allen, Walker Kessler and Giannis Antetokounmpo. Decent company for a 6-foot-5 sophomore.

Through 14 games, Harper is averaging 18.3 points, 5.5 rebounds, 4.7 assists and 1.0 steals in 31.5 minutes per game, shooting 55% inside the arc, 34% from long distance and 87% from the charity stripe. The list of players to average 18-4-4 for a full season by their age-20 season is just six names long : Magic Johnson, LeBron James, Tyreke Evans, Dončić, LaMelo Ball and Cooper Flagg. Of that group, only Magic shot at least 50% from the field, as Harper is right now.

There's a 7-foot-4 caveat to that, of course. With the exception of rookie Magic playing alongside MVP Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, those other preternatural playmakers didn't have a gravitational force like Wemby pulling attention away from them and opening up opportunities to slash, score and create. But opportunities only matter insofar as you can capitalize on them, and Harper continues to make the most out of his privileged position, perpetually pressuring the defense and looking for all the world like an All-Star in the making — sooner rather than later.

11. There are still some kinks to work out …

It's not all beer and Skittles in San Antonio, though. As lights-out as the new-look starting lineup has been, moving Harper into the first five has led to some predictable ripple effects in the second unit. The Spurs' reserve corps has a negative net rating for the season , and has — as you might expect — been significantly worse in the minutes when Luke Kornet checks in for Wembanyama , struggling to score even with at least one of Fox, Castle or Harper on the floor.

Some of those struggles might be mitigated by the introduction of Harris, whom the Spurs signed to a two-year, $31 million contract in free agency , and who's yet to play after suffering a left calf strain during training camp . But Johnson will have to shuffle his rotation to make space for the veteran forward. What impact might that have on the minutes and productivity of the likes of Julian Champagnie, whose quick-trigger 3-point shooting has proven so vital for this iteration of the Spurs? Or Keldon Johnson, the reigning Sixth Man of the Year? Or Harrison Barnes, one of just two Spurs (along with Champagnie) knocking down at least 40% of his triples? Or second-year power forward Carter Bryant, whose ongoing development is a clear priority for San Antonio's future plans?

If Harris isn't able to hit the ground running — specifically by spacing the floor at a high level, as he did for Cade Cunningham in Detroit last season — it could throw some sand into the gears of a Spurs offense that has been humming despite not generating a ton from beyond the arc. San Antonio ranks just 26th in the league in the share of its shots that come from beyond the arc, and right around league-average in 3-point shooting accuracy .

That lagging 3-point attempt rate clearly hasn't hampered the offense's effectiveness thus far; some of it stems from the fact that the Spurs hammer the rim as frequently and effectively as nearly any team in the league. After finishing above league-average in 3-point attempt rate the last three seasons , though, you'd imagine Johnson would prefer to find ways to get a few more up — if for no other reason than to be prepared to have multiple styles to play when the postseason comes around and defensive game plans prioritize clogging the paint to take away Wembanyama's rolls to the rim and the three-headed guard monster's driving lanes to the basket.

If opposing defenses are able to congest the interior and force the Spurs to sing for their supper from outside, it'll bring to the forefront perhaps the most significant issue carrying over from last season: whether they have enough bankable 3-point shooting.

As it stands, the entire starting five — Wembanyama, Fox, Castle, Harper and Vassell — currently sits below 35% from deep for the season. Reigning Sixth Man of the Year Johnson is at 22.7%; erstwhile unicorn-turned-indoor cat Kornet hasn't attempted a long ball since April of 2025 . The Spurs can make a lot of magic happen in tight confines, thanks to the size and brilliance of Wembanyama, and the speed, skill and force of their guards. If hardly anybody in the rotation can make a jumper when they need to, though, problems will arise.

12. … but they could be even better than this.

Those issues — the bench minutes, the shooting, etc. — are not exactly surprises to the Spurs. They're well aware that they've got room to improve.

"If we felt like we're the best version of ourselves at this point in the season, we'll be in trouble," Keldon Johnson recently told reporters .

As excellent as their offense has been, the Spurs have actually underperformed their expected shot quality by the league's fifth-largest amount, according to Synergy Sports Technology's tracking — and all four teams above them in that ranking (Charlotte, Milwaukee, Utah, Chicago) have been terrible, without the talent to meaningfully bridge the gap between expectation and reality. That's certainly not the case in San Antonio.

If Wembanyama (35% from deep last season, 32% this season), Vassell (38% last season, 31% this season) and Johnson (36% last season, 23% this season) tick up toward their previous marks, and any of Fox, Harper or Castle nudge up toward league-average on their looks, this Spurs offense might have another level to reach. Honestly, it might even if only one of those guys keeps the arrow pointed north. You can probably guess which one.

"I can still do more," Wembanyama told reporters after his 52-point masterpiece against the Mavericks. "I mean, my shots weren't falling tonight and that forces me into a style of play that is exhausting. I can do it. I mean, the proof is here. I can do it, but I can be much better if my shots fall. I know it's just a matter of time."

If that happens — if the shots start to fall, the offense soars and the defense remains elite — then it might just be a matter of time before the Spurs are hoisting the Larry O'Brien Championship Trophy, too.

articles.title: New NBA Rumors Link Tom Thibodeau, Mark Jackson to Kings Amid Doug Christie Hot-Seat Buzz
articles.summary: The Sacramento Kings "would prefer not to fire" head coach Doug Christie, but they might be considering alternatives all the same, according to The Stein Line's Marc Stein.
articles.body:
The Sacramento Kings "would prefer not to fire" head coach Doug Christie, but they might be considering alternatives all the same, according to The Stein Line's Marc Stein .

Stein reported Tom Thibodeau and Mark Jackson are "potential down-the-road candidates" to replace Christie.

Appearing on Sactown Sports 1140 last week, The Athletic's Sam Amick said Sacramento is "sensitive to the idea that Darius Acuff potentially would have three different head coaches in his first season."

The Kings are almost certainly going to miss the playoffs this season. Acuff's development should be one of their bigger focuses, even if it comes at the cost of losing more games in the short term.

Things could hit a critical mass, though, with Stein noting Sacramento is on pace to go 6-76. That's not an ecosystem in which you want your young cornerstone to operate.

There are few coaches you'd trust to stabilize things more than Thibodeau. He has a .579 career winning percentage, and his teams have posted a losing record just three times in his 13 years as a head coach.

Jackson is more of a wild card given how long he has been out of the game. His last season with the Golden State Warriors was 2013-14. And while his tenure immediately preceded the start of Golden State's dynasty, the internal atmosphere wasn't in a great place when he exited.

In the event Christie is dismissed, you'd expect more coaches to enter the mix. If he's willing to take on the challenge, Thibodeau is probably the biggest fish Sacramento could land.

articles.title: Draymond Green Says 'Pressure' on Yaxel Is 'Unfair' with Steph Curry Out Injured for Warriors
articles.summary: As the Golden State Warriors look for offensive solutions having lost three straight games since Stephen Curry's injury, Draymond Green thinks Yaxel Lendeborg is being put in a difficult spot.
articles.body:
As the Golden State Warriors look for offensive solutions having lost three straight games since Stephen Curry's injury, Draymond Green thinks Yaxel Lendeborg is being put in a difficult spot.

Following the Warriors' 115-94 loss to the New Orleans Pelicans on Monday, Green told reporters the "pressure" on Lendeborg to be their primary driver of offense is "unfair" for a player this early in his rookie season:

"It's unfair to him to try to make him step into Steph's role 13 games into his career. So, depend on him like we need to, but lower what we're expecting out of him to allow him to then just flow into it. I think, right now, we're putting too much pressure on him, and it's tough to deal with in game 13, 14."

Biggest NBA Surprises and Disappointments 🏀

Head coach Steve Kerr echoed Green's sentiments that they have asked a lot of Lendeborg right out of the gate and how it could serve to help him as he figures out how to navigate NBA defenses:

"He's a rookie. This is his first year, and we're putting an enormous responsibility on his shoulders, and so, he has to go through this. There's no way around it. You can't cheat your way through that. You have to feel the highs and the lows, and you heard his comments the other night — he cares about all this stuff, which is a great sign. But you have to learn how to manage that and how to learn from each situation."

When Curry went down with a torn oblique in the first quarter of Golden State's loss to the Houston Rockets on Nov. 11, it was understandable for Kerr to turn to Lendeborg in an attempt to make up for some of the loss in scoring.

The No. 11 pick in the 2026 NBA draft, Lendeborg entered the league as an old rookie at 24 years of age. He looked the part of a physically mature player with 21.7 points on 51.8 percent shooting (42.6 percent from three), 7.4 rebounds and 3.7 assists per game in his first 12 starts.

Lendeborg understood the difficult task in front of him with Curry expected to miss at least one month. He told reporters prior to Friday's game against the San Antonio Spurs his confidence level was "six out of 10 that he could fill the void, but admitted the other four points were reserved to wonder "am I going to be able to live up to it?"

The results through two games have been ugly for Lendeborg and the Warriors. He has shot 10-of-36 from the field with three more turnovers (seven) than assists (four).

Golden State has lost to the Spurs and Pelicans by a combined 57 points. The Warriors trailed by 24 after the first quarter in both games.

As Green pointed out, no one else on the Warriors is helping the situation. Brandin Podziemski, who signed a $110 million extension before the start of the season, has scored 23 points on 5-of-18 shooting in the last two games.

LJ Cryer got a shot with the starting unit against the Pelicans after dropping 20 off the bench against the Spurs. He finished with seven points on 2-of-10 shooting from the field.

Lendeborg figures to get more comfortable over the course of the season. He is just being put in an impossible spotlight because the Warriors are a marquee team and few players in NBA history have ever been able to do what Curry is capable of.

articles.title: New Dejounte Murray Trade Rumors Reveal Market for Guard, Pelicans' Stance on Potential Move
articles.summary: Despite his request to be traded from the New Orleans Pelicans, veteran guard Dejounte Murray reportedly may have to wait a while before finding a new home.
articles.body:
Despite his request to be traded from the New Orleans Pelicans, veteran guard Dejounte Murray reportedly may have to wait a while before finding a new home.

Sports Illustrated 's Chris Mannix reported that after talking to "several rival team officials," the sense is that Murray's trade market "will be lukewarm at best." Mannix added that the Pelicans "want value back in return" and "don't just want to offload him."

Murray started the season with respectable averages of 17.8 points, 5.8 rebounds and 6.0 assists in four October games, but his numbers dropped to 10.0 points, 3.6 rebounds and 3.2 assists in five games this month. ESPN's Brian Windhorst recently reported that the Pelicans sent him home following his trade request, and his value has diminished around the league.

Mannix went on to add that Murray is believed to be "interested" in a trade to the Phoenix Suns, who are known to be in need of a starting point guard. However, he added that it's "unclear how interested Phoenix is." He's owed $33 million this season and has a player option for $31 million in 2027-28, so two team officials told Mannix that they would "ask for a first-round pick to absorb Murray's contract."

The Pelicans reportedly aren't looking to give up draft assets in addition to losing Murray. New Orleans acquired him from the Atlanta Hawks before Joe Dumars joined the front office as head of basketball operations, and the team won't want to lose him for nothing after giving up Dyson Daniels and two first-round picks in the trade. Mannix noted that the Pelicans are "happy to move off" the 30-year-old because second-year star Jeremiah Fears is considered "the point guard of the future."

It sounds like Murray is no longer viewed as a top target around the league, so he could have to wait until closer to the Feb. 12 trade deadline before he's moved.

articles.title: Nikola Jokic Calls Out Nuggets After Loss to Suns, Comments on DeMar DeRozan in New Video
articles.summary: Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokić told reporters during his press conference after his team's 117-105 home loss to the Phoenix Suns on Monday that unnamed team members need to accept their roles in pursuit of victory.
articles.body:
Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokić told reporters during his press conference after his team's 117-105 home loss to the Phoenix Suns on Monday that unnamed team members need to accept their roles in pursuit of victory.

"We need to know who we are and what can bring us to the victory," Jokić said (5:26 mark).

"And don't be bored, or don't be ungrateful for your role, or maybe you just need to do one thing the whole game, or maybe you just need to whatever.

"Because I think for me, the victory is the most important thing. So you just need to accept and then be the best possible guy or player in that role."

This has been an up-and-down season for the 7-5 Nuggets. They did show their potential in a road win over the 10-4 Memphis Grizzlies, but they also have lost all five of their games by eight or more points.

Of note, six-time All-Star DeMar DeRozan is enduring some struggles in the early going. The 37-year-old (and 18-year veteran) is averaging 9.2 points on 40.0 percent shooting (14.3 percent from three).

Jokić was asked about integrating DeRozan into the team (2:57 mark).

"I mean, you just need to know who he is, and special players you need to know and learn how to play with them," Jokić began. "Some players you need a little bit more time, some players you need a little bit less time, but I think you just need to learn how you can give him the advantage, because he doesn't need a lot. He just needs a little bit advantage. And I think guys, me, whatever, and Deebo just need to learn how to create those advantages."

The Nuggets endured an ugly game. Phoenix outscored Denver by 16 points over the final three quarters. The Suns also out-rebounded Denver 51-35. The Nuggets committed 18 turnovers and shot just 9-of-30 from three-point range. Meanwhile, Phoenix made 16-of-36 threes (44 percent).

It was an off-night for DeRozan, who had just two points on 1-of-6 shooting.

Of course, this season is still in the early stages, and DeRozan is a potential Basketball Hall of Famer who has averaged 21.0 points per game over nearly two decades in the league.

There's plenty of time for him to turn this around and for the Nuggets to start playing consistently good basketball.

Denver will look to get back on track soon enough, although the road won't be easy in the short-term as the 11-3 Boston Celtics and 11-4 Houston Rockets arrive into town on Wednesday and Friday, respectively.

articles.title: NBA Panic Meter: Can Pelicans fix this mess? Do Suns need to make a move?
articles.summary: We're about a month into the season, the perfect time to check in on some underperforming situations around the league.
articles.body:
We're about a month into the season, the perfect time to check in on some underperforming situations around the league. Are these overreactions given the small sample sizes? Or are there deeper things at play that will continue to be magnified? Let's take a look.

Stop me if you've heard this before, but New Orleans is a mess.

Players taking laps around the court in the midst of a near-60-point loss. Cryptic messages in pressers. Star players retweeting reports of a trade request. (I'm not joking, this is the craziest thing I've ever seen since covering this sport.)

ESPN broke news of Dejounte Murray's wishes to depart from the franchise, but the growing consensus among rival executives is that Murray's value has gotten to a point where he cannot be moved unless there is quality draft compensation attached to him, sources told Yahoo Sports. The whispers of growing discontent behind the scenes related to the accelerated hires of head coach Jamahl Mosley (this season) and by proxy, executive vice president of basketball operations Joe Dumars (last season), had only grown louder amid the Pelicans' recent six-game losing streak (they ended the streak Monday, defeating the Steph Curry-less Warriors), sources said, citing confusion as to why extensive searches were not conducted on either front.

As it pertains to Murray, according to sources, the thinking is simple. His unhappiness and hope for a new environment is not new and has been discussed privately since last season, with a growing sense that his reluctance to return earlier from his January 2025 Achilles tear was in hopes of being moved at last year's deadline. But it was rather difficult to define a market for an injured player (Murray returned later that month). The decision to draft Jeremiah Fears last summer was another clear indicator that New Orleans was open to moving in another direction, which sources said upset Murray — echoing similar sentiments to his departures from San Antonio and Atlanta.

"What a f***ing mess," one high-ranking executive from a rival team said. "No one wants to touch him."

The veteran guard is a polarizing talent when healthy and engaged, but finding the harmony of both has been quite the challenge over his decade-long career.

The Suns opting to go ZeroPG in their starting lineup (word to Matt Harmon) is going about exactly as you might have expected. Phoenix started the season losing five of their first six games and is currently a game under .500. But it hasn't been its 25th-ranked defense that has been the talk of the town. It's the utter lack of cohesion and control at the other end.

A glance at metrics would show you the Suns actually are 11th in overall (and half-court) offensive efficiency, which is juiced somewhat, thanks to some funky transitional opportunities (the Suns are third in points off turnovers because of an aggressive on-ball scheme that generates mistakes ). They're just outside the bottom 10, though, in passing rate, assist points created and potential assists .

And they're losing the Jalen Green-at-point-guard minutes badly. Phoenix has been outscored by 137 points in the 346 minutes Green has been on the floor, according to PBP Stats. Quite simply, it hasn't gone to plan. When Green was initially traded as part of the blockbuster move sending Kevin Durant to Houston, sources say one of Green's reasons for optimism was the consistent word from the Suns that he would be given on-ball opportunities — an element of his game that gradually faded with the emergence of Amen Thompson. The numbers, at least in theory, backed it up; Green was a low-turnover, high-usage guy that showed promise in spots as a creator when called upon.

But part of the charm with Green's playmaking was it came within the flow of his aggression, utilizing his speed and power. Factor into some offseason roster moves, notably inserting Miles Bridges (who isn't one to turn down a drive), more reliance on Devin Booker and less on Green, and you have yourself a player being shoehorned into a role that doesn't suit him or the team. Green's drive rate is the lowest it's been in four seasons and he's converting shots and holding on to the bal l at career lows. (He's also shooting around 64% from the charity stripe this month and has yet to crack 30% from deep.) And it's led league executives to believe the 24-year-old, with one year left on his deal and a $36 million player option for next year, is attainable — and that Green wouldn't be opposed to a better fit elsewhere. It's unclear at this stage what Green's current market looks like, but New Orleans, which has kept tabs on him since he was in Houston, just might be paying more attention.

I'll admit, this might feel a tad bit nitpicky.

The Heat are riding a five-game winning streak, have won seven of their last nine, and sit just one game off third in the East after a horrendous start to the season. Klay Thompson has effectively doubled his scoring output this month, Miami just dropped 137 on a top-10 defensive unit and the Giannis Antetokounmpo-Bam Adebayo tandem seems to be working out some early kinks.

The Heat are a stone's throw outside the bottom-five in defensive rating, 29th in opponent 3-point and midrange conversion rate, and 29th in half-court defense.

With any metric — especially this early — some noise is expected. We also don't typically have a decent grasp on a team until about 15-20 games. So yes, there will be some bad opponent shooting luck .

But part of Miami's selling point as a contender was the versatility of Antetokounmpo, Adebayo and Davion Mitchell, and some of those concessions meant assuming it was its offense, not defense , that would need time to jell. Given the uneven start, two central questions surrounding Miami's defensive output are: have the schemes changed since Giannis' arrival, and is this working?

For starters, the Heat are throwing out a lot less zone than normal. Last season, nearly 17% of their defensive possessions featured a zone defense, which has dropped over 10%(!), according to Synergy tracking data. (Miami was also allowing a little less than a point per possession on such instances, now sitting closer to league average.) They're switching more than normal but not getting the same results: bottom 10 in points allowed (that's not solely a Giannis/Bam issue, but they're not fully absolved).

Looking more closely, issues remain with that tandem. Opponents are shying away from the rim when both are on the floor (in their most-used lineup), but the ones that dare to attack are converting over 70% of chances. In addition, when they give up 3s, opponents are shooting 50% from deep. Hardly the recipe for success. Antetokounmpo and Adebayo are also contesting less , not getting enough ball pressure and just not looking aggressive in passing lanes (their "Big 3" on defense are hovering around 50% in steals and deflection rates).

I'm not overly worried, but I'm also cooling down on my prediction that this will end up as a top-five defense by season's end.

I understand why everyone (including this committee of one) was so high on Charlotte heading into the year. There was always going to be a risk in trading LaMelo Ball and his cerebral playmaking, undoubtedly the heartbeat of one of the NBA's premier offenses — but the Hornets seemed equipped to handle it. Charles Lee, one of the brightest young minds around, was still in charge. So were Brandon Miller and Kon Knueppel, to whom the keys were to be given, as well as Naz Reid's unicorn floor spacing and Coby White's tantalizing projections as lead ball-handler.

So how does this team find itself five games under .500 and ranked 30th in offense and half-court efficiency?

A few reasons. Knueppel has played just six minutes, re-aggravating the same left hamstring that kept him sidelined during the preseason. White just returned this month after suffering a calf strain and continues to be on a minutes restriction. Miller has shown no confidence in handling the lion's share of touches ceded by Ball and Miles Bridges, averaging the highest usage and lowest shot-making efficiency of his career thus far, making just 28 of 110 3-point attempts.

And the misuse of Reid has been puzzling to say the least. Over his last three seasons in Minnesota, Reid's 3-point volume accounted for around half of his offensive usage. That has been sliced down to less than 40%, which ranks in just the 34th percentile among forwards , with only 7% of his attempts coming from the corners (14th percentile). It's been a work in progress to say the least, which explains why Reid's frustration, combined with Lee's no-nonsense approach, led to a benching earlier in the month.

But this is as much of a problem of Lee's as it is the new pieces in place. The Hornets have become too predictable and stagnant, not enough rim presence and no real control, either. Being one of the best offensive rebounding and worst ball-security teams is like taking two steps forward and four back. Getting Knueppel back will solve quite a bit — as will simplifying Miller's role and expectations — but it doesn't look good in Charlotte right now.

articles.title: Duncan Robinson, Pistons' second-leading scorer, to miss at least a week with left quad strain
articles.summary: The injury derails a stellar start to the season for Robinson, who has stepped into a larger offensive role in place of the injured Jalen Duren.
articles.body:
Detroit Pistons forward Duncan Robinson has suffered a left quadriceps strain and will be re-evaluated in a week, the team announced Tuesday .

Robinson sustained the leg injury during the team's game against the Miami Heat on Saturday. He exited the contest with 4:17 remaining in the second quarter, was deemed questionable to return with left thigh soreness , and never checked back in, finishing with 10 points on 3-for-8 shooting in 17 minutes. The Pistons went on to lose the game, 137-117 — their largest loss of the season.

The injury derails what's been a stellar start to the season for Robinson, who has stepped into a significantly larger offensive role than anticipated in the absence of injured All-NBA center Jalen Duren. The 32-year-old sharpshooter enters Tuesday's action as Detroit's second-leading scorer behind superstar point guard Cade Cunningham, averaging a career-high 17.4 points per game, shooting 43.1% from 3-point range on more than nine attempts a night.

After topping 20 points five times in 77 appearances for Detroit last season , Robinson has already done it five times in his first 12 games this season . He's leveled up as a scorer despite subsisting on one of the toughest shot diets of any player in the league — and outperforming that shot diet by one of the league's largest margins .

Maybe the most surprising area in which Robinson is excelling? In transition. He is eighth in the NBA in total fast-break points on the young season, behind a slew of speed demons (Tyrese Maxey, Ayo Dosunmu, Dylan Harper, Jeremiah Fears) and giant playmaking forwards (Giannis Antetokounmpo, Jalen Johnson, Kevin Durant). Thanks to his knack for sprinting the floor at every change of possession and his comfort with being able to stop on a dime, catch and fire accurately, Robinson has been extremely efficient at attacking with the advantage, shooting 22-for-34 from the field — including 12-for-21 from 3-point range — to produce a whopping 1.61 points per possession on the transition plays he finishes, according to Synergy Sports Technology's tracking.

Heading into this season, only 22 players who'd played enough minutes in a season to qualify for the minutes-per-game leaderboard had ever launched at least 14 3-point attempts per 100 possessions of floor time, according to Stathead. Of that group, only five had ever knocked down at least 40% of their long balls on that kind of volume: Stephen Curry (who's done it five times, naturally), Klay Thompson (duh), Donte DiVincenzo (who kind of learned how to be a Splash Brother during his stint in the Bay), Sam Merrill and Malik Beasley ... whose off-ball movement, floor-spacing gravity and quick-trigger release was a key component in the resurgence of Detroit's offense before the, um, unpleasantness .

Now, Robinson occupies that role for the Pistons, and he's playing it to the hilt, splashing in 43.1% of his triples while launching 14.5-per-100 . Combine that with a newfound penchant for drawing contact that's seen him turn in by far the highest free-throw attempt rate of his career, and Robinson has posted a true shooting percentage (which factors in 2-point, 3-point and free-throw accuracy) of .658 — his best mark since his breakthrough 2019-20 season in Miami, and a near-top-10 mark among players to log at least 300 minutes this season , just below Luka Dončić.

"We've got guys that can really gun it and are being encouraged to shoot," Robinson recently told reporters . "The way we can defend and then get out in transition and attack the paint, being able to make teams pay from behind the line is big as well."

That level of volume and accuracy, combined with near-perpetual off-ball motion — only 14 players have covered more ground on offense per game this season, according to Second Spectrum tracking — make Robinson the kind of player that defenses can't afford to ignore. He ranks a somewhat-surprising seventh in the NBA's gravity metric — a stat aiming to quantify "how much a player pulls defenders towards them [...] how much attention they draw compared to what the spacing on the floor predicts." The amount of defensive attention that Robinson's drawing thus far this season? It slots in right between Thompson and Damian Lillard.

It's not just that Detroit's 3-point attempt rate increases with Robinson perpetually ready to fire away off the catch, either. The Pistons have shot significantly better at the rim in Robinson's minutes, too. If you have to have a defender staying in his hip pocket everywhere he goes, that's one fewer help defender who can sink in to plug up driving lanes, pack the paint and protect the cup.

"He carries so much weight and so much gravity," Pistons coach J.B. Bickerstaff recently told reporters . "The shots that he's making aren't always easy shots, so those frustrate defenses as well. Now, it's going to force people to put more bodies on him, and that's just going to keep opening up the game for everybody else. He's doing a great job, obviously."

That impact has shown up in a big way for the Pistons, who enter Tuesday's matchup with the West-leading San Antonio Spurs at 8-4, in third place in the Eastern Conference. Thanks in part to how that gravity warps opposing defenses, and in part to how Robinson's been scorching the nets himself, the Pistons have scored 119.3 points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions with Robinson on the floor, according to Cleaning the Glass — a near-top-five rate of offensive efficiency. For the season, Detroit has scored 8.8 more points-per-100 more with Robinson on the floor than off it — the largest offensive on/off swing of any Piston to play significant minutes this season.

"He's perfecting his craft," Cunningham recently told reporters . "He's the top in the world at it. He just makes everybody's job easier."

And without him — for the next few games, at least — everybody in Detroit's job gets a little bit harder.

articles.title: LeBron James Names NBA Players with 'Prettiest' Jump Shots, Shouts Out Klay Thompson, Bradley Beal
articles.summary: LeBron James has set countless records and accomplished just about everything there is to accomplish in the game of basketball. But there are plenty of players who he still admires and appreciates.
articles.body:
LeBron James has set countless records and accomplished just about everything there is to accomplish in the game of basketball. But there are plenty of players who he still admires and appreciates.

He was asked on the "Mind the Game" podcast to list the players he thought, off the top of his head, had the prettiest jumpers he ever saw and listed Ray Allen, Steve Nash, Klay Thompson, Bradley Beal, Mitch Richmond, Devin Booker, Chris Mullen and Mark Price (4:50 mark).

LBJ Picked Up 'Bad Habits' Trying to Imitate MJ

LeBron Reacts to Passing Kidd on Assist List

James then broke down his own evolution of his jumper.

"My shooting journey is, like, watching Michael Jordan," he told Nash (9:00 mark). "But the thing I didn't realize was how balanced Jordan was. ... I saw the fadeaway, so when I started to see that I had some athletic genes, I maybe picked up some bad habits in my shooting because I could emulate that. I was shooting fadeaways as like a freshman in high school. And I would make them, but I didn't realize that I was picking up bad habits. Because I didn't study, 'OK, M.J.'s doing that but you're not even seeing on balance he is. He's been doing this for years and years and years and you're just doing it because you're trying to emulate him.'"

James acknowledged that even to this day, he has a slight lean back on his jumper. Not that it's kept him from being the NBA's all-time leading scorer or anything.

articles.title: LeBron James Says He Picked Up 'Bad Habits' Trying to Imitate Michael Jordan's Iconic Fadeaway
articles.summary: Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has been following in Michael Jordan's legendary footsteps throughout his iconic career, but he couldn't copy his idol's favorite move.
articles.body:
Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has been following in Michael Jordan's legendary footsteps throughout his iconic career, but he couldn't copy his idol's favorite move.

While discussing his basketball journey on the Mind the Game podcast with co-host Steve Nash, James revealed that he used to try to mimic Jordan's signature fadeaway jump shot, but he eventually realized that he wasn't getting it right.

"My shooting journey is literally like watching Michael Jordan. But the thing I didn't realize is how balanced Michael Jordan was. I saw a fadeaway. So when I started to see that I had some athletic genes, I maybe picked up some bad habits in my shooting because I can emulate that," James said (9:04 mark). "So I was shooting fadeaways as like a freshman in high school, and I would make them, but I didn't realize that I was picking up bad habits along that time because I didn't study the fact that, OK, yeah, MJ is doing that, but you're not even seeing how on balance he is. You have no idea that, or he's been doing this for years and years and years, and you're just trying to pick it up because you're trying to emulate him."

LeBron Reacts to Passing Kidd on Assist List

James is one of the greatest athletes the NBA has ever seen, but it took him some time to become a reliable jump-shooter. While he couldn't match Jordan's fadeaway, he found his own combination of moves that helped him become the league's all-time leading scorer.

Still, James admitted that Jordan's influence remains in his 24th year in the NBA, as he finds himself unnecessarily fading away the same way he did as a youngster.

"And still to this day, some of it is still in my shot. [I'm leaning back] right off the top," James said with a laugh.

articles.title: España hace Carrera camino del EuroBasket 2027
articles.standfirst: La pívot brilla en el triunfo de la selección ante Croacia en el tercer partido de las Ventanas
articles.summary: La pívot brilla en el triunfo de la selección ante Croacia en el tercer partido de las Ventanas
articles.body: España puso pie y medio en el proximo EuroBasket, a disputar en el verano de 2027, tras su brillante triunfo ante Croacia, 72-91. Con su partido en Porec, España ha logrado el objetivo de sumar las tres victorias en las tres primeras jornadas de la segunda fase de clasificación para la cita continental. Ante la República Checa ya en febrero, podría sellar su billete de forma virtual e incluso matemática. España jugó un partido muy coral sobre todo a partir del segundo cuarto, aunque por encima de todas las jugadoras estuvo Raquel Carrera, autora de 22 puntos y cinco rebotes. La jugadora del Valencia Basket fue un verdadero dolor de muelas para el juego interior croata y aprovechó en muchas ocasiones los dos contra uno sobre Iyana Martín para tirar con mucha comodidad. También dio un nivel excelente Iyana Martín, otro partido, otro clinic. Esta vez en asistencias. Rozó el doble-doble con 12 puntos y 9 asistencias. Tirando menos que en otros partidos se dedicó a dirigir y repartir juego. Pero hubo más protagonistas, como Helena Pueyo, 12 puntos con 4/4 en triples (España acabó con un fabuloso 14/24 desde el arco), como María Araujo (11 puntos) o como Paula Ginzo, que hizo 9 puntos. La selección jugó en un pequeño pabellón en Porec con muy poco público y ante un rival que desde el inicio sabía que era inferior. Las croatas aguantaron bien en el primer cuarto, cuando España dio su peor versión sobre todo en el tiro (6-18 en tiros de campo), para un 20-15 en el parcial del cuarto que daba cierta esperanza al equipo croata. Con Carrera e Iyana en plena producción, España dio la vuelta al partido en la salida del segundo asalto con un 0-10 de parcial (20-25). En el final de ese segundo acto se empezó a ver que España era muy superior. En cuanto aceleró, se marchó en el marcador, 29-39 a 2:42, gracias a la zona española que propuso Méndez y que frenó la producción de jugadoras como Begic (que acabó con 22 puntos), Dojkic (17) o Cave (16), las únicas entre las croatas a cierto nivel para competir. Aunque con cinco minutos de partido en el tercer cuarto Croacia se acercó (44-48), dos triples, de Iyana y Pueyo, volvieron a disparar a España, esta vez sí de forma definitiva. La ventaja no hizo más que crecer hasta los 19 puntos finales del 72-91. Al margen del tiro de tres España superó ampliamente a Croacia en rebotes, 26-37 y repartió 27 asistencias, demostrando lo bien que habían compartido el balón las jugadoras de Méndez que firmaron ante las croatas el mejor partido de las Ventanas, al menos en el que más jugadoras estuvieron involucradas. Las Ventanas, en las que España ha ido de menos a más, se cierran con esos tres triunfos que casi aseguran la presencia de la actual bronce Mundial en el próximo EuroBasket.
